name: Tsishaath Nootka
confidence_why: Stonham 1999, Wilson 1986 and Davidson 2002 all give the same Tseshaht rule (stress the first syllable unless it is light and the second is heavy, never beyond the second syllable) and Kim 2003 reports the same for Ahousaht, but the three Tseshaht analyses all rest on Sapir's transcriptions, which Davidson 2002 finds fit the rule in only 73-84% of tokens, and the sources differ on whether a coda nasal makes a syllable heavy.
catalog_citation: Stonham, John. 1999. Aspects of Tsishaath Nootka Phonetics & Phonology. Munich: LINCOM Europa (LINCOM Studies in Native American Linguistics 32). Chapter 6 'Stress', pp. 57-61.
catalog_locator: pp. 58-60 (of the scan; pp. 59-60 rendered to PNG and read, p. 58 from the saved scan); domain statement p. 58 (§6.2); weight criterion p. 59; rule (10) p. 60; VʔV caveat p. 60; secondary stress pp. 60-61 (§6.3).
catalog_quote: [p. 58] In Tsishaath Nootka stress assignment the domain of primary stress is the first two syllables of the word (i.e., the first foot). [p. 59] As we can see from these data, the stress always appears on the first or second vowel of the word, regardless of the presence of long vowels further on. It is also the leftmost of two long vowels which is assigned the stress in the case where there are two in the first two syllables of the word (egs. 4 c,d,g). ... The examples below indicate that when there is an obstruent in the coda, there is no effect on the placement of stress. ... All of this seems to suggest that for the purposes of stress assignment, either a long vowel or a vowel-sonorant sequence consist of two moras and, accordingly, attract the stress from a mono-moraic syllable. [p. 60] The domain of the stress rule for Nootka is the first two syllables, or the first foot. The rule can thus be described as: (10) Tsishaath Stress Rule: Stress the leftmost heavy syllable within the first foot; if both syllables are light, stress the leftmost one in the first foot.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is confined to the first two syllables of the word (the initial foot). Heavy syllables are those with a long vowel or a short vowel plus a tautosyllabic sonorant (nasal) coda. Stress the first syllable if it is heavy, or if both of the first two syllables are light; stress the second syllable only when the first is light and the second heavy (#LH́). Long vowels later in the word do not attract primary stress. Davidson 2002:25 (Tseshaht text data) states the same rule in terms of vowel length only ('first syllable short and second long -> second syllable; otherwise first syllable; first syllable accented by default'); Kim 2003:163 gives the same long-vowel rule for Ahousaht.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stonham 1999:60-61: beyond the first foot there are 'further stresses … of a secondary nature'; 'secondary stress occurs on alternating syllables from the primary stress, following the foot structure of the language', with the caveat that this 'remains to be clearly worked out'. Contrast Kim 2008:70 (Ahousaht): 'there is no secondary stress'. Werle 2010:16 lists Stonham 1994a, Waldie 2003, Werle 2007 as reporting secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stonham 1999:60: VʔV sequences attract stress (primary or secondary) regardless of position and may even outrank heavy syllables ('a possible hierarchy of weight'); 'much work remains'. Davidson 2002:25-26: rule fits 206/245 unambiguous tokens (84%) in Sapir 1924; accent inconsistently transcribed across tokens of the same word; evidence contradictory on whether coda nasals count as heavy (Stonham's data yes, Sapir 1924 examples no). Kim 2003:163: no evidence for moraic coda consonants in Ahousaht — weight = long vowel only. Werle 2010:16 (citing Waldie 2003): variable stress in #LL and #HH words in Ahousaht; Kim 2008:70 (citing Stonham 1999, Thorp 2004): with two long or two short initial syllables stress may fall on either.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word), stress window = first two syllables; Stonham's data are Sapir's 1910-14 Tseshaht field transcriptions of texts, Davidson's a single transcribed text (Sapir 1924); Kim's are elicited Ahousaht forms from her own fieldwork. Stress is not contrastive (predictable from weight) per all sources; Werle 2010:16 notes prominence is contrastive only in the Northern Wakashan languages Haisla and Heiltsuk.
new_statements.identity_note: Stonham 1999 describes the Tseshaht/Tsishaath dialect (Glottolog tsis1239, Barkley Sound) from Sapir's 1910-14 field notes; Davidson 2002 §2.5 also uses Tseshaht data (Sapir 1924). Kim 2003 (and Carlson, Esling & Fraser 2001, Waldie 2003) describe Ahousaht (ahou1237, Central); Kim agrees on the first-two-syllable, long-vowel-sensitive rule but finds no evidence that coda sonorants are heavy in Ahousaht, and Werle 2010 (citing Waldie 2003) reports variable stress in #LL/#HH words there. Rose 1981 (Kyuquot, Northern) gives no stress statement. The catalog entry should be keyed to the language nuuc1236 with the Tseshaht/Ahousaht split noted.

new_statements.quote: [p. 288] In Nootka, stress falls on the first syllable, unless it is light and the second syllable is heavy, in which case the second syllable receives the stress. There are no secondary stresses marked in the data, and stress never falls anywhere but on the first two syllables. [p. 289] The stress rule of Nootka cannot be "stress the first heavy syllable in a word", which would be the parallel version of the Kwakwala rule. When both of the first two syllables are light, stress falls on the first even when there are other heavy syllables later in the word. [...] In Makah, stress falls on the first syllable if it is heavy, and on the second syllable if the first is light.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as Stonham 1999 (leftmost heavy in the first foot, else first syllable); adds that heavy = long vowel or short vowel + nasal, that variable vowels pattern as short, that there is no secondary stress, and a metrical (single initial foot) analysis. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field, which this fills.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is confined to the first two syllables (a single non-iterating initial foot): the first syllable is stressed unless it is light (short vowel) and the second is heavy (long vowel, or short vowel plus nasal), in which case the second syllable is stressed; when both are light the first is stressed by default, even if heavier syllables follow. Variable vowels count as short. Data are Nootka proper, Tsishath dialect (p. 283), from Sapir 1924 and Sapir & Swadesh 1939.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'There are no secondary stresses marked in the data' (p. 288); Wilson treats the loss of secondary stress as a Nootkan innovation vs. Kwakwala (p. 290).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Nootka. The Makah rule differs when both initial syllables are light (Makah stresses the second, p. 289). No data on Nitinat or smaller Nootka dialects (p. 289).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Tsishaath/Tseshaht dialect: Wilson p. 283 draws his Nootkan data from 'Nootka proper (Tsishath dialect)' via Sapir 1924 and Sapir & Swadesh 1939; Davidson p. 4 states the dissertation covers 'Makah and the Tseshaht dialect of Nuuchahnulth (Nootka)' and his accent data are Sapir's 1924 Tseshaht text. Wilson p. 289 also gives the Makah rule (second syllable when both initial syllables are light) and says no stress data exist for Nitinat or other Nootka dialects; neither of those is this language.

new_statements.quote: [p. 24-25] Sapir's transcription shows that accent placement in Nuuchahnulth is governed by a rather different rule from that found in Makah [...] The apparent basic rule in Nuuchahnulth is, if the first vowel of a word is short and the second vowel is long, the accent falls on the second syllable; otherwise the accent falls on the first syllable. In other words, the first syllable is accented by default. [p. 25] This rule works in most cases, but there are exceptions. Quick tabulation shows the rule accounts for 206 of 284 word tokens [...] 73%). [n. 10] Accent in Makah is stress accent, which is probably the case in Nuuchahnulth as well.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as Stonham 1999 and Wilson 1986 (first syllable by default; second only if first short and second long). Adds a token count of fit against Sapir 1924, the observation that the transcription is inconsistent, the open question of coda-nasal weight, and the statement that the accent is probably stress accent. Explicitly about the Tseshaht dialect (p. 4: 'Makah and the Tseshaht dialect of Nuuchahnulth (Nootka)').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (probably stress accent) falls on the second syllable only when the first vowel is short and the second is long; otherwise on the first syllable, which is the default. Based on Sapir's 1924 Tseshaht text 'The Rival Whalers' (284 word tokens); presented as a preliminary rule of thumb that fits 73% of tokens (84% once unaccented words and one Ditidaht name are set aside).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Nuuchahnulth; for Makah, endnote 10 notes possible secondary prominences on long vowels, of unclear status.
new_statements.exceptions: 78 of 284 tokens in Sapir 1924 do not fit (many are words with no accent marked or tokens of the Ditidaht name); accent is inconsistently marked across tokens of the same word; evidence is contradictory on whether a coda nasal makes a syllable heavy for accent (Stonham's field-note examples say yes, several Sapir 1924 words such as 'foot' and 'the one at the bow' say no); 'Further research is required' (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Tsishaath/Tseshaht dialect: Wilson p. 283 draws his Nootkan data from 'Nootka proper (Tsishath dialect)' via Sapir 1924 and Sapir & Swadesh 1939; Davidson p. 4 states the dissertation covers 'Makah and the Tseshaht dialect of Nuuchahnulth (Nootka)' and his accent data are Sapir's 1924 Tseshaht text. Wilson p. 289 also gives the Makah rule (second syllable when both initial syllables are light) and says no stress data exist for Nitinat or other Nootka dialects; neither of those is this language.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: Stonham 1999 (existing statement), Wilson 1986 and Davidson 2002 all give stress on the first syllable unless it is light and the second is heavy, restricted to the first two syllables. One sub-point differs: Wilson (p. 288) and Stonham 1994 (as cited by Davidson) count a short vowel plus nasal coda as heavy, whereas Davidson (p. 26) finds Sapir 1924 words in which a second-syllable coda nasal does not attract accent from a short first syllable and calls the evidence contradictory. Davidson also qualifies the rule as a rule of thumb fitting 73-84% of Sapir's tokens, with inconsistent accent marking in the source text.

sources.note: p. 145: 'Nuu-chah-nulth assigns stress on either of the first two syllables of the word, i.e., the first foot, and the weight of the syllable is a crucial factor … Stress falls on the 1st syllable of the word, unless it is light and the 2nd is heavy, in which case stress falls on the 2nd syllable' (citing Sapir & Swadesh 1939, Wilson 1985, Howe 1996, Stonham 1999); p. 163 (own analysis): 'Syllable weight … is involved only in stress assignment: stress is assigned on the initial syllable in a foot except when the second syllable is heavy i.e. includes a long vowel' — no evidence for moraic cod…

sources.citation: Werle, Adam. 2010. The Phonology of Wakashan Languages. Ms., University of Victoria (survey). §4.2 'Word prominence', p. 16.
sources.note: p. 16: 'In the southern languages, primary stress is on the first or second syllable of the word. Long vowels contribute to syllable weight, but coda nasals in Nuu-chah-ulth are the only consonants that do so … All southern languages stress the first syllable if it is heavy (#H́L, #H́H), and the second if it is heavier than the first (#LH́). But Nuu-chah-nulth gives two initial light syllables trochaic stress (#ĹL)'; reports variable stress in #LL and #HH words in Ahousaht (Waldie 2003) and secondary stress (Stonham 1994a, Waldie 2003, Werle 2007). Secondary survey.
